column4: The section's dictionary note on 89:9 evokes a man who crosses lands repeatedly; this ayah warns against being deceived by disbelievers' movement through the lands, since their apparent worldly mobility ends in loss.
The preceding 3:196 warns against the disbelievers' movement through lands; this ayah supplies that movement's real endpoint, only brief enjoyment and then a wretched abode.
The section contrasts a journeying person with one fixed by attachment; these stay-behinds rejoice in remaining after the Messenger and dislike striving with their property and lives.
The preceding 9:38 asks why believers cling to earth instead of the Hereafter; this ayah gives the warning's consequence: failure to go forth brings punishment and replacement by another people.
The section cites 7:176's person who clings to earth and follows desire; this preceding ayah explains his turn by saying he had been given signs but cast them off and followed Satan.

The section evokes a traveler crossing lands and recalls ancient powers; this ayah asks people to travel the earth and see the end of earlier peoples, whose strength and traces did not protect them from judgment.

The section joins travel across lands to old settled powers; this ayah asks people to travel and look at the fate of earlier peoples who cultivated the land more extensively, yet were destroyed after rejecting messengers.

This repeated travel-and-observe formulation says earlier peoples had greater numbers, strength, and traces in the land, but their earnings did not avail them, connecting monumental settlement to what cannot be retained.

The section's roaming traveler passes through lands marked by earlier powers; this ayah likewise asks people to travel and consider the end of those before them, showing that greater strength did not let them escape God.
The section names former powers and their lands; this ayah asks people to travel and observe how God destroyed earlier peoples, making the route through the land a lesson in their end.
The section hears a traveler crossing countries; after describing messengers sent to every community, this ayah tells people to travel through the land and see the end of those who denied them.
The section names ancient settled lands and rock-cut places; this ayah describes ruined towns, an abandoned well, and a lofty palace, giving the traveler concrete traces of vanished settlement.
The preceding 22:45 shows ruined towns and abandoned structures; this ayah asks whether people have traveled the land and gained understanding from what happened, linking the traveler to the ruins.
The section's country-crossing traveler is told in another passage to travel through the earth and see the end of the guilty, directly turning movement across lands into a view of their fate.
The section's traveler ranges from country to country; this ayah asks people to travel the earth and observe the end of earlier peoples, making travel an encounter with what remains after them.

The section's traveling person moves across the earth; this ayah explicitly joins travel through it with observing how creation began and how God will bring forth the later creation, linking the route to origin and return.

The section describes intense love of money and fixation on earthly possessions; this ayah names people who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God's path, setting up the wealth that becomes punishment in 9:35.
The preceding 9:34 names hoarded gold and silver; this ayah says that same wealth is heated and used to brand its owners, turning what they clung to into a bodily burden at judgment.

The section joins love of possessions to heaviness and binding; this ayah says what people withhold will be encircled around their necks on the Day of Resurrection, making attachment itself a restraint.

The section's dictionary note says a garment wears out and a mount is consumed by travel; this ayah pictures worldly life as vegetation that becomes dry debris scattered by wind, a specific image of what seemed substantial passing away.

The section says testing can wear down what a person thinks is his; this ayah compares worldly life to growth that yellows and becomes debris, contrasting temporary possession with the lasting Hereafter.
The section's 89:21 context crushes the earth at the end; this ayah gives a parallel scene in which the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed in one blow.
The section connects the ground's final crushing with return; this ayah describes the mountains moved, the earth laid bare, and all people gathered, joining altered landscape to final assembly.
The section's earth is crushed at the end; this ayah answers a question about the mountains by saying the Lord will blow them away, extending the scene from earth to its fixed high landmarks.
The preceding 20:105 says the mountains will be blown away; this ayah says the land is left as a level plain, completing the landscape's removal of height and support.
After 20:105 and 20:106 describe mountains removed and a level plain, this ayah says no crookedness or elevation will remain, making the emptied terrain explicit.
The section ends with entry among God's servants; this ayah describes the Garden entered by the righteous and their righteous families, with angels coming to them from every gate.
The preceding 13:23 shows the Garden and its entrants; this ayah gives the angels' welcome of peace for their patience and calls it an excellent final home.
The section's last stage is entry into the Garden; this ayah shows the angels welcoming the good at death with peace and the command to enter Paradise.
The section presents a soul arriving tranquil and welcomed; this ayah describes the angels reassuring those who remained steadfast and giving them glad tidings of the Garden.
The section's final soul is pleased and pleasing as it returns to God; this ayah joins God's pleasure with the believers' pleasure and promises them lasting gardens.
The section ends with entry among God's servants; this ayah describes the early believers as a group with whom God is pleased and for whom He has prepared gardens.

The section moves from being tested toward a tranquil soul and entry into the Garden; this ayah describes earlier believers enduring hardship and upheaval before asking when God's help will come, making trial part of the passage toward that end.
The section's call is to return to the Lord; when the deniers see the Fire, they instead wish to be sent back to worldly life so they can believe, reversing the direction of return.
The preceding 6:27 gives the deniers' wish to return; this ayah says that if they were sent back, they would repeat what they had been forbidden, closing that imagined route back.
The section's return is a completed journey to the Lord; here the deniers, seeing the punishment, wish they could return to become believers, a late reversal that cannot restore the road.
The section describes the soul returning to its Lord; this ayah gives the condemned person's wish for another return so he might become one of the good-doers.
The preceding 39:58 gives the wish for another return; this ayah answers that God's signs had already come and were denied, giving the reason the request cannot reopen the journey.
The section's return call leads the soul to God; those who forgot the final meeting instead ask whether they can be returned to act differently, a specific reversal of that completed passage.
The section's journey reaches its final return; this ayah gives wrongdoers' request for a short delay so they can answer the messengers, another too-late attempt to resume earthly life.
